title: How to Build a Datadog to Snowflake Integration
summary: Datadog Snowflake integration lets you monitor your warehouse without writing code. Set up the connection in minutes following the setup guide.
body_markdown:
## Building one Snowflake to Datadog workflow in Activepieces


Build it as a trigger, a Snowflake query step, and a Custom API Call that posts to Datadog, tested step by step before you publish.


Other automation tools connect these two apps as well.


Activepieces fits when you want open source and self-hosting: its core is MIT-licensed, and the Snowflake and Datadog integrations used here sit among the 750 integrations counted directly from the open source monorepo on GitHub, in the packages/integrations/community directory, where **roughly 60% were contributed by the community** rather than the vendor.


### Step 1: Create the workflow and pick the trigger


Create a new flow and choose a Schedule trigger so the flow runs on a fixed interval.


A schedule is the safer starting point because it makes the cost of each run predictable: every run is one query against Snowflake, so a short interval means more warehouse time billed to you.


Pick the longest interval your alerting can tolerate.


Inside the builder, a flow is a vertical chain, trigger on top, with the selected step's settings in the right panel.


In the screenshot below, a Discord "New Message" trigger exposes Connection, Limit and Channel fields, and every trigger in your flow will have the same kind of panel.


Note the "Publish" button and the unpublished-changes banner: nothing you build runs live until you publish.


### Step 2: Connect Snowflake and Datadog


Add the listed Snowflake step and create its connection from the step's Connection dropdown. Use a Snowflake user whose role can read only the tables you're reporting on.


Then add a Custom API Call step for Datadog, with the endpoint and your API key in the header, as described above. Keep the key in the step's header field and out of any query text, since step inputs show up in run logs.


Once both steps are connected, step 3 is mapping the fields. Write the query in the Snowflake step, and select only the columns Datadog needs.


Then, in the Custom API Call body, insert each column from the query step's output into the matching field of the Datadog payload.


1. Choose the metric or event name Datadog will receive.
2. Map the value column from the Snowflake output.
3. Map a timestamp column so Datadog plots the point when it happened, not when the flow ran.
4. Add any tags you filter on.


Before anything goes live, step 4 is testing and publishing. Test each step in order, starting with the trigger and then the query. Confirm the output shows the rows you expect before the Datadog step uses it.


Run the Custom API Call last and check that the point appears in Datadog. If the response is an authorization error, recheck the header first. Once it passes, click Publish.
